subject: English
description: Definite vs indefinite, zero article, fixed phrases

questions.stem: Choose the correct form: 'She is ____ honest woman.'

options.option_text: a
an
the
no article

questions.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a silent H — the sound is a vowel. Use 'an' before vowel SOUNDS (not letters). Similarly: 'an hour', 'an MP', but 'a university' (yu-niversity), 'a European' (yu-ropean) — silent vs sounded starts.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: A
An
The
No article

questions.explanation: Use 'the' for unique entities: the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth, the universe. One-of-a-kind objects always take definite article.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: He went to ____ bed at 10 p.m.

options.option_text: a
the
no article
an

questions.explanation: With habitual 'go to bed / go to school / go to church / go to hospital (BrE)' → zero article when meaning the intended purpose. 'Go to THE bed' would mean the specific physical piece of furniture.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: a
the
no article
an

questions.explanation: Single-word country names use ZERO article: India, China, France, Japan. EXCEPTIONS with 'the': plural / union countries (The United States, The United Kingdom, The Netherlands, The Philippines, The Maldives). Named rivers DO take 'the' (the Ganga).
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: a
an
the
no article

questions.explanation: MBA begins with the LETTER M (consonant) but the SOUND 'em' (vowel sound). Hence 'an MBA'. Same for MA, MP, MSc. SPELLING is irrelevant; pronunciation matters.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correctly used article: '____ Himalayas are in northern India.'

options.option_text: A
An
The
No article

questions.explanation: Mountain ranges take 'the' (The Himalayas, The Alps, The Rockies, The Western Ghats, The Andes). Individual peaks do NOT — 'Mount Everest' (no article). Groups of islands (The Andamans) also take 'the'.
questions.subject: English

options.option_text: a
the
an
no article

questions.explanation: Musical instruments take 'the': 'play the guitar / piano / violin / sitar'. Sports, however, take ZERO article: 'play cricket / football / chess'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: He was celebrated as ____ one-of-a-kind musician whose compositions transcended all genres.

options.option_text: a — 'one' starts with the consonant sound /w/, not a vowel sound
an — 'one' begins with the vowel letter 'o', so 'an' is needed
the — definite article for a musician already introduced in context
no article — unique descriptions following 'as' require no article

questions.explanation: 'One' is pronounced with the consonant sound /w/ (identical to 'won'), so 'a' is correct, not 'an'. The a/an rule is entirely based on the first sound of the following word, not its spelling. Option B is the most common mistake: students see the vowel letter 'o' and apply the wrong rule.

questions.stem: She stood on top of ____ highest peak in the Western Ghats and could see three states.

options.option_text: a — indefinite article used for non-specific tall mountain peaks
an — used before adjectives that begin with certain vowel sounds
the — definite article is obligatory before superlative adjectives
no article — superlative adjectives can function without any article

questions.explanation: 'The' must precede superlative adjectives (highest, tallest, fastest) because they identify a singular, unique entity. 'A' is the most tempting wrong answer but would incorrectly imply one of many high peaks rather than the single highest one. Superlatives never appear with 'a/an'.

questions.stem: ____ number of applications received for the scholarship this year was far greater than expected.

options.option_text: A — 'a number of' means 'several'; would correctly require plural verb 'were'
The — refers to a specific definite count; correctly pairs with singular 'was'
An — 'number' is frequently confused with vowel-starting quantifier words
No article — quantifier nouns at sentence start take no determiner

questions.explanation: 'The number of' refers to a specific, countable quantity and governs a singular verb ('was'). 'A number of' means 'several/many' and governs a plural verb ('were'). The singular verb 'was' in the sentence is the key grammatical clue. Option A is the most tempting error: students habitually use 'a number of' without noticing the verb-agreement signal.

questions.stem: After the bridge was washed away, all cargo was moved ____ sea to reach the coastal warehouses.

options.option_text: by a sea — indefinite reference to a particular stretch of water nearby
by the sea — idiomatically means beside or along the coastline, not via it
by sea — zero-article fixed phrase expressing the mode of transport
across sea — preposition 'across' replaces the need for an article here

questions.explanation: Fixed transport idioms — by sea, by air, by road, by rail, by hand — always use zero article. 'By the sea' is the most tempting wrong answer but it means 'near/beside the sea,' not 'via the sea as a route.' The zero-article rule applies uniformly across all means-of-transport phrases in English.

questions.stem: Her grandfather reads ____ Times of India along with two regional newspapers every single morning.

options.option_text: a — indefinite article for general reference to any newspaper copy
The — newspaper and periodical titles conventionally require 'the'
no article — proper nouns like newspaper names never need an article
an — 'Times' opens with a vowel-letter, so 'an' should precede it

questions.explanation: Established newspaper and magazine titles carry 'the' as a permanent part of their identity — The Times of India, The Hindu, The Economist. Option C is the most tempting distractor because newspaper names look like proper nouns, which normally take no article. However, periodical titles are a well-known exception to that rule.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses the article correctly with a personal title?

options.option_text: The Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud delivered the landmark ruling yesterday.
Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud delivered the landmark ruling yesterday.
A Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud delivered the landmark ruling yesterday.
An Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud delivered the landmark ruling yesterday.

questions.explanation: When a title immediately precedes a personal name, the article is dropped entirely: 'Chief Justice Chandrachud', 'President Droupadi Murmu', 'Prime Minister Modi'. Option A is by far the most tempting wrong answer because 'The Chief Justice' is grammatically correct — but only when the personal name does NOT follow. The moment the name appears, the article disappears.

questions.stem: The welfare programme was specifically designed to uplift ____ elderly and provide them with better healthcare.

options.option_text: elderly — zero article; adjectives functioning as nouns need no article
an elderly — singular indefinite reference to just one older individual
the elderly — 'the + adjective' forms a collective plural class noun
a elderly — indefinite singular, parallel to how 'a child' is used here

questions.explanation: 'The + adjective' (the elderly, the poor, the blind, the rich) creates a collective plural noun referring to an entire class of people. 'The elderly' here means 'elderly people as a group', which is confirmed by the plural pronoun 'them' later in the sentence. Option B ('an elderly') refers to a single person and contradicts 'them', while bare 'elderly' without any article is ungrammatical in this direct-object position.
